idiom_name: index-signature interfaces with type guards (or a schema validator)
implementation_notes: TypeScript puts static types back on top of the same dynamic objects: declare the view as an interface with the properties you know plus an index signature (for example [key: string]: unknown) for the rest, and the compiler checks every access while the runtime keeps plain objects. Structural typing means a view is a type rather than a class, so the Document/AbstractDocument/trait roles collapse into type declarations and a narrowing predicate. Types are erased, so data from outside the program still needs a type guard or a schema validator (zod, valibot) at the boundary; prefer unknown over any in the index signature, since any re-enables exactly the unchecked access the pattern exists to avoid.
pitfalls: Interfaces, index signatures and assertions are erased at runtime, so a view cast applied to unchecked data fails only when a property is used - validate at the boundary.
A string index signature forces every declared member to match the index type, and an `as` assertion bypasses the excess-property checks an object literal would have received.
Typing the index signature as any instead of unknown silently re-enables unchecked access everywhere and defeats the narrowing the views depend on.
